historical_timeline.summary: Scurvy found at the Discovery's winter quarters after a sledge journey; seal meat added to sledging rations.
Tobacco running out on the southern journey; tried tea leaves.
Red gums and slight ankle swelling recorded at a medical examination on the southern journey.
Returned to the ship with swollen legs, sore gums, and weeks of lassitude.
Married; naval commands and Admiralty work between the expeditions.
Organizing and raising funds for the British Antarctic Expedition from its London offices.
Reached the South Pole; a rival expedition had been there first.
Frostbite of the right foot recorded on the return march.
Last journal entry, in the tent on the Ross Ice Shelf; died of cold and hunger about this date.

claims.statement: Robert Falcon Scott was born on June 6, 1868, at Plymouth, Devon, into a seafaring family, and joined his first Royal Navy ship when he was 13.

source_links.locator: born in Devon; seafaring family; first ship at 13

claims.statement: He led the Discovery expedition to the Antarctic from 1901 to 1904.

In October 1902, at the Discovery's winter quarters, scurvy was found after a sledge party returned from the western journey; the expedition's surgeon then examined everyone on board and found signs in a good many men, in most only the merest indication, and the outbreak was over by about October 20. Scott arranged to replace part of the sledging pemmican with cooked seal meat.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Documents the sledging scurvy of the Discovery expedition; no other man is named here.

source_links.locator: volume I, chapter on the outbreak of scurvy, October 4 to 20, 1902

claims.statement: On the southern sledge journey (November 1902 to February 1903) the party examined gums and legs every Sunday. When one companion developed angry-looking gums in late December 1902, they stopped eating bacon and increased the seal-meat ration, and Scott recorded that the scurvy symptoms lessened.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Fresh seal meat as the remedy is documented; the companion's health is mentioned only as the trigger for the change of diet.

source_links.locator: volume II, entries of December 21, 22 and 28, 1902

claims.statement: At a thorough medical examination on the southern journey on January 14, 1903, Scott recorded that he himself had "distinctly red gums, and a very slight swelling in the ankles." Two days later, on a double ration of seal meat, his gums were much cleaner and his leg vastly improved; by the last days of the journey he wrote that their scurvy had been advancing again and that his ankles were considerably swollen.
claims.clinical_interpretation: His own documented signs of scurvy in his mid-thirties.

source_links.locator: volume II, entries of January 14, 16 and early February 1903

claims.statement: After the southern party returned to the ship in February 1903, Scott wrote that he had both legs much swollen and very uncomfortable gums, and an extraordinary lassitude, physical and mental, that lasted many weeks before he returned to a normally vigorous condition.
claims.clinical_interpretation: His own account of recovery from scurvy and exhaustion.

source_links.locator: volume II, chapter on the return of the southern party

claims.statement: In his account of the Discovery expedition he wrote that scurvy was then believed to be ptomaine poisoning from tainted meat. A modern historian of medicine notes that many British doctors of the time accepted this view and overlooked the experiments of Holst and Frølich on dietary deficiency, so medical advice given to him before his second expedition would probably not have helped him prevent scurvy.
claims.clinical_interpretation: The ptomaine statement is documented in his own book; the judgment about what advice could have achieved is a retrospective interpretation.

source_links.locator: volume I, remarks on the nature of scurvy

claims.statement: On the southern journey, on December 20, 1902, he wrote that his tobacco supply was so low that he had been trying tea leaves, which were "nothing less than horrid."
claims.clinical_interpretation: Documented tobacco use; anchors the synthetic pipe-smoking history.

claims.statement: After the Discovery expedition the needs of the naval service called him to the command of battleships and to confidential work at the Admiralty, and five years passed before he resumed Antarctic work. In 1908 he married the sculptor Kathleen Bruce; they had one son.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Career and household context; no health facts about his family are recorded.

claims.statement: On November 24, 1909, he wrote from the offices of the British Antarctic Expedition at 36 and 38 Victoria Street, London, that the Pole was at the forefront of the campaign for raising funds but that scientific work would not be neglected.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Places him in London organizing and funding the expedition before the modern episode begins.

claims.statement: The Terra Nova left the Roath Basin at Cardiff on June 15, 1910, with Scott and members of the British Antarctic Expedition on board.
claims.clinical_interpretation: The synthetic episode ends before this date. Where and when he finally joined the ship for the voyage south is given differently in the comments on the source page and is not used.

claims.statement: He reached the South Pole on January 17 to 18, 1912, and found that a rival expedition had already been there.
On the return march, on March 18, 1912, he wrote that his right foot had "gone, nearly all the toes," and on March 19 that amputation was "the least I can hope for now."
claims.clinical_interpretation: After the episode. His own documented frostbite.

claims.statement: All five men of the polar party died of cold and hunger. Two died earlier on the return march; Scott and the two remaining companions died in their tent about 11 miles short of a depot of food and fuel. His last journal entry, dated March 29, 1912, records a continuous gale since March 21, fuel and food exhausted, and ends "For God's sake look after our people." A search party found the tent on November 12, 1912.
claims.clinical_interpretation: After the episode. The date of his death is taken from the last entry and is approximate.

source_links.locator: deaths from cold and hunger; 11 miles from the depot; found on November 12

claims.statement: His original diaries of the second expedition, from October 18, 1910 to March 29, 1912, are held by the British Library as Add MS 51024-51042.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Locates the primary record; not a clinical claim.

claims.statement: A historian of medicine concludes that scurvy may have contributed to the general ill health of the polar party in 1912, but that their deaths were more likely caused by a combination of frostbite, malnutrition and hypothermia.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Retrospective interpretation; the record does not diagnose scurvy in 1912.

claims.statement: Physiologists reviewing the expedition conclude that rations of a different composition, giving more energy for the same weight, might have saved some of the party, and that more vitamin C, though hard to achieve at the time, could have improved their chances.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Retrospective interpretation; used to frame the modern nutrition plan.

claims.statement: Atmospheric scientists comparing the party's temperature records with modern automatic weather stations found that daily minimum temperatures from late February to March 19, 1912 were on average 10 to 20 °F below those measured in the same region and season since 1985, and that this cold likely contributed substantially to the party's exhaustion and frostbite.

synthetic_episode.teaching_objective: Primary care and wilderness and expedition medicine for a 41-year-old naval officer, five months before he leads a long Antarctic expedition with a winter in a hut and months of hauling sledges on foot: a structured pre-expedition medical assessment (cardiovascular risk and fitness, dental, hearing, vision, vaccinations); an elevated office blood pressure confirmed as stage 1 hypertension with home readings, lifestyle measures first, and an angiotensin receptor blocker chosen over a thiazide or a beta-blocker for cold and dehydration, with sick-day rules; stopping pipe tobacco with varenicline, because nicotine raises frostbite risk; nutrition planning for energy needs of man-hauling in extreme cold and vitamin C to prevent the scurvy he had on an earlier journey; frostbite and hypothermia prevention and field first aid training; altitude on the polar plateau; sleep and mental health in isolation with screening and a support plan; and an evacuation and communication plan. Built on the Wilderness Medical Society frostbite (1908), hypothermia (1903) and altitude (1908) guidelines, the 1909 AHA/ACC high blood pressure guideline, the CMID hypertension monograph, and the USPSTF tobacco, depression and anxiety recommendations.

hpi.narrative: Mr. Scott returns two weeks after his pre-expedition assessment, on the day of his consultation with Dr. Nwankwo-Lund. He took two home readings morning and evening for seven days with a validated upper-arm monitor; the average of the 28 readings is 138/88 mmHg, with no single reading above 150/95. He has no headache, chest pain, breathlessness, or visual change. He stopped his pipe on his quit date a week ago and takes varenicline, with mild nausea after the morning dose. He has started to use less salt. He asked whether a diagnosis of high blood pressure would count against him in leading the sledge journeys; he was told it is common, treatable, and not in itself a reason to stop him.

assessment_plan.assessment: The elevated office reading at intake is now confirmed by home readings: a seven-day average of 138/88 mmHg is stage 1 hypertension. Intake tests show no target-organ damage or secondary cause: sinus rhythm without left ventricular hypertrophy on the ECG, creatinine 0.92 mg/dL (eGFR 107), potassium 4.2 mmol/L, sodium 140 mmol/L, fasting glucose 92 mg/dL, HbA1c 5.3%, TSH 2.1 mIU/L, and LDL cholesterol 122 mg/dL. No urine sample was given at intake. His ten-year cardiovascular risk is low: about 5% by the Pooled Cohort Equations counting him as a smoker, and below the 7.5% threshold by the PREVENT equations, so the guideline advises lifestyle measures for three to six months before medicine. Dr. Nwankwo-Lund agrees, and advises an angiotensin receptor blocker, rather than a thiazide or a beta-blocker, if medicine is needed, started at least four weeks before departure

hpi.narrative: Mr. Scott returns four weeks after his consultation. His home readings over the last week average 136/86 mmHg. He has cut his salt and trains three times a week, walking fast with a weighted pack and running, and has lost about a kilogram. He has not smoked his pipe for five weeks; the nausea on varenicline has gone. He gave the urine sample a week ago. He has had his dental examination and cleaning, his hearing test, and an eye examination. He sleeps six to seven hours and his mood is good.

referral.question: Pre-expedition assessment of a 41-year-old naval officer who will lead a long Antarctic expedition sailing in about five months, with a winter in a hut and sledge journeys of several months on foot. Please advise on his fitness and any further testing, the management of a newly raised blood pressure in that setting, nutrition and scurvy prevention, cold injury and altitude precautions, mental health and sleep in isolation, and an evacuation and communication plan
referral.pertinent_history: Well and fully active, with no cardiac or respiratory symptoms. Office blood pressure 144/90 mmHg today; one week of home readings requested to confirm. Pipe smoker, about 25 g of tobacco a week since his early twenties; varenicline started today with a quit date in one week. Alcohol within low-risk limits (AUDIT-C 3). On a long polar sledge journey in his mid-thirties he had scurvy, with red gums and swollen ankles and legs, which improved on fresh seal meat, and he had weeks of lassitude after returning; he recovered fully. Examination: BMI 24.2, heart and lungs normal, no edema. ECG: sinus rhythm, no left ventricular hypertrophy. Sodium 140 and potassium 4.2 mmol/L, creatinine 0.92 mg/dL (eGFR 107), fasting glucose 92 mg/dL, HbA1c 5.3%, total cholesterol 196, HDL 52, LDL 122 and triglycerides 110 mg/dL, TSH 2.1 mIU/L, hemoglobin 15.1 g/dL. PHQ-9 3, GAD-7 4. Dental, hearing and eye checks are being arranged. He is anxious that nothing should stop him leading the sledge journeys himself
questions: Is he fit for a long polar expedition with heavy sledge hauling, and does he need any further cardiac or other testing?
If his blood pressure is confirmed as raised, how and when should it be treated, given cold, dehydration and long marches?
What nutrition plan, including energy and vitamin C, will prevent the scurvy and weight loss of his earlier journey?
What frostbite, hypothermia and altitude precautions and training does the party need?
How should his mental health and sleep be supported in months of isolation and polar light?
What evacuation, communication and medical kit plan is appropriate?

consultant_note.history: Mr. Scott, a 41-year-old naval officer, is seen at the request of Dr. Harrow-Mbeki before he leads an Antarctic expedition that sails in about five months. He is well, with no chest pain, breathlessness, palpitations, fainting, or exercise limitation, and walks fast every day. Home readings since his intake visit average 138/88 mmHg. He stopped his pipe a week ago on varenicline. On a long sledge journey in his mid-thirties he developed red gums and swelling of the ankles and legs, which improved within days on fresh seal meat and returned when the meat ran short; after the journey he had swollen legs, sore gums and weeks of exhaustion before a full recovery. This expedition will include a voyage south, a winter in a hut with weeks of darkness, and sledge journeys of up to several months hauling loads on foot, partly on a high plateau, with no evacuation possible for much of the year
consultant_note.data_reviewed: Dr. Harrow-Mbeki's intake note and results: ECG sinus rhythm without left ventricular hypertrophy; sodium 140, potassium 4.2 mmol/L, creatinine 0.92 mg/dL (eGFR 107), fasting glucose 92 mg/dL, HbA1c 5.3%, LDL cholesterol 122 mg/dL, TSH 2.1 mIU/L, hemoglobin 15.1 g/dL; PHQ-9 3, GAD-7 4, AUDIT-C 3. Home blood pressure log: 28 readings over seven days, average 138/88 mmHg. No urine albumin result yet

Regular rhythm; normal heart sounds; no murmur; no radio-femoral delay
Clear to auscultation bilaterally

assessment.display: Fitness for a long polar expedition
assessment.assessment: He is fit to take part, including in long sledge journeys. He has no symptoms and a low ten-year cardiovascular risk, so an exercise test or echocardiogram would add little and is not needed; a graded training program before departure will prepare him better. Dental, hearing and eye checks are worth completing, because none can be fixed in the field

Confirmed by home readings, with no sign of target-organ damage on the tests so far; the urine albumin test is still needed. At his low risk the guideline advises three to six months of lifestyle measures first, which fits his timetable. If the home average stays at or above 130/80 at about three months, an angiotensin receptor blocker such as losartan is the best choice for the expedition: a thiazide adds to salt and water loss with cold diuresis and long marches, and a beta-blocker can worsen cold extremities and blunt the response to exercise. It should start at least four weeks before departure, so that electrolytes and creatinine can be checked two to four weeks after starting, with written sick-day rules for vomiting, diarrhea and dehydration

assessment.display: Personal history of scurvy; nutrition for man-hauling
assessment.assessment: His earlier scurvy came from months without fresh food, and his recovery on seal meat fits vitamin C deficiency. Scurvy can appear after one to three months of very low intake, so a reliable daily source is essential on preserved rations. Man-hauling in extreme cold needs roughly 5,000 to 6,500 kcal a day, more than earlier sledging rations gave, and energy-dense fat is the lightest way to carry it

Frostbite and hypothermia are the main environmental threats on the journeys. Prevention, early recognition, and correct field treatment (rewarming only when refreezing can be prevented) matter more than any medicine. The polar plateau is high, and the cold makes its effect on the body greater than its height suggests, so altitude illness is possible on the ascent

assessment.display: Mental health and sleep in isolation
assessment.assessment: PHQ-9 3 and GAD-7 4 are minimal. The polar winter, constant daylight on the journeys, crowding, and months of separation from his family are known strains; a plan made now is more useful than a crisis plan later

recommendations: No exercise test or echocardiogram; a graded training program with weighted-pack walks and endurance work before departure

Blood pressure: lifestyle measures now; home readings before each visit; urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio; if the home average is still 130/80 or higher at about three months, start losartan, at least four weeks before departure, with electrolytes and creatinine in two to four weeks and written sick-day rules; avoid thiazides and beta-blockers
Stop tobacco completely, with varenicline and counseling, because nicotine narrows skin blood vessels and adds to frostbite risk; no nicotine products in the field

Nutrition: about 5,000 to 6,500 kcal a day on man-hauling journeys with a high fat share; weigh weekly in the hut; fresh seal meat when available; vitamin C 250 mg daily from tablets packed in every sledging ration when no fresh food is available, well above the recommended 90 mg and far below the 2,000 mg upper limit; a weekly check of gums and legs

Cold injury: a wilderness first aid course before departure for him and the sledging parties, covering frostbite and hypothermia prevention, rewarming in water at 37 to 39 °C only when refreezing can be prevented, ibuprofen for frostbite, gentle handling and insulation of hypothermic casualties, and casualty packaging in a sledge
Altitude: gradual ascent to the plateau, with acetazolamide in the medical kit to treat acute mountain sickness

Mental health and sleep: repeat PHQ-9 and GAD-7 before departure; a fixed routine, bright light in the polar winter and eye masks in constant daylight, a monthly self-check, and a named person in the party to talk to

Evacuation and communication: a written plan with satellite messaging where it reaches, the seasonal evacuation windows, and a medical kit, medicine supply and medical summary sized for a year without resupply
Dental examination and cleaning, audiometry, and an eye examination with spare glasses and glacier glasses before departure
